specPoints.text: understand the nature of the following intermolecular forces: i London forces (instantaneous dipole-induced dipole) ii permanent dipole-permanent dipole interactions iii hydrogen bonds

primer.text: Between neighbouring molecules sit three ranks of attraction, none of them true covalent bonds. This note separates the bonds inside a molecule from the weaker pulls between molecules, then ranks the trio: fleeting induced dipoles, permanent dipoles, and the special case where hydrogen meets oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine. Master the ranking order now; it explains boiling points, solubility and melting behaviour later.

lessons.title: Forces within and between molecules
lessons.opening: Every molecule is held together inside by covalent bonds, yet a liquid or solid only coheres because of much weaker pulls acting across separate molecules. This lesson splits the two families apart, names the three intermolecular types, and sets the strength ladder that every later topic climbs.
keyPoints: Intramolecular forces operate inside one molecule and are ordinarily covalent bonds built from shared electron pairs.
Single, double, triple and co-ordinate bonds all count as intramolecular forces.
Intermolecular forces act between neighbouring molecules and are far weaker than the bonds inside them.
The three intermolecular types are induced dipole-dipole, permanent dipole-dipole, and hydrogen bonding.
A hydrogen bond reaches only about one tenth of a covalent bond's strength, which keeps the ladder honest.

low.restatement: Inside a molecule the shared pairs form strong covalent bonds; between molecules sit three weaker attractions that decide how easily the substance melts or boils.
low.analogy: Covalent bonds are the stitching that holds each shirt together, while intermolecular forces are the Velcro dots letting shirts stick to each other in the drawer.
low.examPointer: Never call an intermolecular attraction a bond when a question asks for force types - keep 'bond' for the covalent links inside the molecule and score the distinction mark.

medium.restatement: The electron pairs shared between nuclei give intramolecular covalent bonding; the between-molecule attractions are ranked induced dipole-dipole, then permanent dipole-dipole, with hydrogen bonding as a strengthened sub-case of the permanent type.
medium.analogy: Picture scaffolding poles welded into one frame (intramolecular) versus magnets letting separate frames cling together (intermolecular) - welding always wins the strength contest.
medium.examPointer: Compare strengths in the order asked: covalent bond, then hydrogen bond, then permanent dipole-dipole, then induced dipole-dipole - inversions cost the mark every session.

check.stem: Which description correctly pairs a force with where it acts?

options.text: Covalent bonds act within a single molecule
options.explanation: Shared electron pairs link atoms inside one molecule, which is the intramolecular setting.

options.text: Hydrogen bonds act within a single molecule
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding links neighbouring molecules, never atoms inside one molecule.

options.text: Induced dipole forces act within the nucleus
options.explanation: Nuclear forces are outside the chemist's classification entirely.

options.text: Intermolecular forces join two atoms into a new molecule
options.explanation: Joining atoms into a molecule is covalent bonding, the intramolecular job.

check.stem: Which set lists the three intermolecular force types?

options.text: Induced dipole-dipole, permanent dipole-dipole, hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: These are exactly the three between-molecule attractions in the strength ladder.

options.text: Ionic, covalent, metallic
options.explanation: Those are the three intramolecular bond classes, not between-molecule forces.

options.text: Single, double, triple
options.explanation: Those grade covalent bond order inside molecules.

options.text: London, metallic, van der Waals
options.explanation: Metallic bonding does not appear in the intermolecular trio.

check.stem: Roughly how strong is one hydrogen bond compared with a covalent bond?

options.text: About one tenth as strong
options.explanation: The hydrogen bond reaches roughly a tenth of a covalent bond's strength, which still beats every other intermolecular pull.

options.text: About ten times stronger
options.explanation: Nothing between molecules outmuscles a covalent bond by that margin.

options.text: Exactly equal
options.explanation: Equality would erase the melting and boiling point patterns the ladder explains.

options.text: About one thousandth as strong
options.explanation: That understates the hydrogen bond badly.

check.stem: Which statement about the strength ladder is correct?

options.text: Induced dipole-dipole is the weakest of the three intermolecular types
options.explanation: Fleeting dipoles give the gentlest attraction, sitting at the ladder's foot.

options.text: Permanent dipole-dipole is the weakest type
options.explanation: Permanent dipoles outpull induced ones at equal size, so they cannot be last.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding is weaker than induced dipole-dipole
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding tops the between-molecule ladder.

options.text: All three types share identical strength
options.explanation: The whole point of the ladder is that the ranks differ.

check.stem: A single, double or co-ordinate bond belongs to which family?

options.text: Intramolecular forces
options.explanation: All of those bond orders are covalent links inside one molecule.

options.text: Intermolecular forces
options.explanation: Between-molecule attractions never come in single, double or co-ordinate varieties.

options.text: Hydrogen bonding
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is one intermolecular type, unrelated to bond order.

options.text: Nuclear attractions
options.explanation: Nuclear forces hold nuclei together, not molecules.

check.stem: State the difference between intramolecular and intermolecular forces, with one example of each.
check.modelAnswer: Intramolecular forces act inside one molecule, for example the covalent bonds sharing electron pairs; intermolecular forces act between neighbouring molecules, for example hydrogen bonding between water molecules.

check.stem: Name the three intermolecular force types in increasing strength order.
check.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole comes first, permanent dipole-dipole second, and hydrogen bonding third as the strongest between-molecule attraction.

check.stem: Explain why boiling a molecular liquid never breaks its covalent bonds.
check.modelAnswer: Boiling only has to overcome the intermolecular attractions between molecules, which are far weaker than the covalent bonds inside each molecule, so the molecules separate intact and no covalent bond snaps.

check.stem: A hydrogen bond carries one tenth of a covalent bond's strength. If a C-H covalent bond stores 413 kJ per mole, estimate the hydrogen bond energy per mole.
check.modelAnswer: One tenth of 413 kJ per mole is 41.3 kJ per mole, so the hydrogen bond ranks far below the covalent bond yet still leads the intermolecular ladder.

lessons.title: Induced dipoles and their relative strength
lessons.opening: Even molecules with no permanent polarity attract each other. This lesson follows the wandering electron cloud that creates momentary dipoles, shows how those moments induce partners in neighbours, and then ranks induced against permanent dipoles when molecule size is held equal.
keyPoints: Induced dipole-dipole forces exist between every pair of atoms or molecules, polar or not.
A shifting electron cloud can pile up on one side, making a temporary dipole that induces a matching dipole next door.
The attracted ends are the positive region of one molecule and the negative region of its neighbour.
Because the clouds never stop moving, the dipoles stay temporary and the forces stay weak.
At equal electron count, permanent dipoles outpull induced ones, so propanone boils higher than butane.

low.restatement: Electron clouds jitter constantly; an accidental lopsided cloud makes a momentary dipole whose positive end draws the negative side of a neighbour, and the cycle repeats everywhere.
low.analogy: Two shy commuters on a swaying bus: one leans accidentally toward the other, who then leans back - the sway keeps creating fresh pairs of lean-ins.
low.examPointer: Say 'temporary dipole induces a dipole in the neighbour' in that order when describing the mechanism - examiners award the sequence.

medium.restatement: Instantaneous asymmetry of the electron cloud gives a fleeting dipole; its electric field polarises the adjacent cloud, and the correlated flicker is the induced dipole-dipole attraction.
medium.analogy: A generator flickering on and off induces current in a nearby coil only while it runs - here the running never stops, so the induced pull persists statistically.
medium.examPointer: When asked to compare isomers or similar molecules, count electrons first: equal electron count means the induced contribution matches, so any boiling gap must come from the next force type up.

check.stem: What creates a temporary dipole in a non-polar molecule?

options.text: Its electron cloud drifts and piles up unevenly on one side
options.explanation: Constant cloud motion concentrates charge momentarily, producing the fleeting dipole.

options.text: Its covalent bonds snap open
options.explanation: Bond breaking is far too energetic and unrelated to fleeting dipoles.

options.text: A permanent charge separation built into the structure
options.explanation: A permanent separation would make the molecule polar, contradicting the premise.

options.text: Its nucleus shifts between the atoms
options.explanation: Nuclei stay essentially fixed while electrons do the moving.

check.stem: Which statement about induced dipole-dipole forces is correct?

options.text: They exist between all atoms and molecules
options.explanation: Every electron cloud can flicker, so every pair feels this attraction.

options.text: They exist only between non-polar molecules
options.explanation: Polar molecules also carry induced contributions on top of their permanent ones.

options.text: They require hydrogen attached to fluorine
options.explanation: That condition describes hydrogen bonding instead.

options.text: They appear only in the solid state
options.explanation: The forces operate in every physical state.

check.stem: Why does the induced dipole in the neighbour form at all?

options.text: The temporary dipole's electric field distorts the neighbour's electron cloud
options.explanation: Charge asymmetry nearby polarises the adjacent cloud, inducing the matching dipole.

options.text: The neighbour copies the dipole by convention
options.explanation: Copying is not a physical mechanism.

options.text: Covalent bonds stretch across the gap
options.explanation: No shared pair bridges separate molecules here.

options.text: Gravity pulls the heavier end round
options.explanation: Gravitational effects are negligible in molecular attraction.

check.stem: Propanone boils higher than butane even though both carry the same electron count. Why?

options.text: Propanone is polar, so its permanent dipole-dipole forces beat butane's induced ones
options.explanation: At equal electrons the induced contribution matches, so polarity decides the winner.

options.text: Butane has more electrons than propanone
options.explanation: The comparison fixes the electron count as equal.

options.text: Propanone has hydrogen bonds
options.explanation: Propanone's oxygen has no attached hydrogen, so no hydrogen bonding occurs.

options.text: Butane is polar
options.explanation: Butane's symmetric hydrocarbon skeleton leaves it non-polar.

check.stem: Why are induced dipoles only temporary?

options.text: The electron clouds never stop moving
options.explanation: Ceaseless cloud motion keeps remaking and erasing the charge asymmetry.

options.text: The molecules stop vibrating in solids
options.explanation: Vibration persists in every state.

options.text: Heat destroys the dipoles permanently
options.explanation: The flicker is intrinsic, not a temperature artefact.

options.text: Covalent bonds drain the dipole
options.explanation: Nothing drains a dipole through a bond.

check.stem: Describe how a temporary dipole induces a dipole on a neighbouring molecule.
check.modelAnswer: The electron cloud drifts to one side giving a temporary dipole, whose electric field pulls the neighbour's cloud into a matching induced dipole, and the opposite ends then attract.

check.stem: State the relative strength of permanent dipole-dipole and induced dipole-dipole forces for small molecules of equal electron count.
check.modelAnswer: Permanent dipole-dipole forces are stronger than induced dipole-dipole forces when the molecules are small and carry the same number of electrons.

check.stem: Explain why larger electron counts raise boiling points through induced forces alone.
check.modelAnswer: More electrons make cloud distortions bigger and more frequent, so the temporary dipoles are larger and the induced attractions stronger, which raises the energy needed to separate molecules.

check.stem: Propanone needs more energy to separate its molecules than butane at equal electron count. If butane's intermolecular energy per mole is 22 kJ and polarity roughly doubles the pull, estimate propanone's figure.
check.modelAnswer: Doubling 22 kJ per mole gives about 44 kJ per mole for propanone, the premium the permanent dipoles charge over the induced baseline.

lessons.title: Permanent dipoles and hydrogen bonding
lessons.opening: Polarity that never switches off changes the game. This lesson follows the permanent dipole-dipole attraction between polar molecules, then meets hydrogen bonding: the supercharged case where hydrogen bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine reaches a neighbour's lone pair.
keyPoints: Polar molecules carry a permanent positive end and negative end because of bond polarity.
Permanent dipole-dipole forces attract the positive end of one molecule to the negative end of its neighbour.
Hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular attraction and a special case of permanent dipole interaction.
It needs hydrogen covalently bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, whose lone pair faces the exposed hydrogen.
Water's oxygen holds two lone pairs, so one water molecule can form two hydrogen bonds.

low.restatement: A molecule with an uneven charge map always attracts its neighbours end to end; when hydrogen sits on oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, the pulled-apart hydrogen bonds to a lone pair nearby.
low.analogy: Bar magnets in a drawer never lose their poles, so they click together the same way every time; hydrogen bonded molecules are the strongest magnets in the set.
low.examPointer: Draw hydrogen bonds as dashed lines running from the lone pair to the delta-positive hydrogen - solid lines or missing ends lose the diagram mark.

medium.restatement: Bond polarity gives a fixed dipole whose ends align across molecules; attaching hydrogen to the most electronegative elements concentrates so much positive character at hydrogen that a lone pair from another molecule completes an unusually strong link.
medium.analogy: A permanently exposed Velcro strip (the delta-positive hydrogen) grabs the nearest loop (the lone pair) - ordinary dipoles only press fabrics together, they never hook.
medium.examPointer: Quote the donor condition exactly - hydrogen covalently bonded to O, N or F - and name the lone pair destination when sketching the link.

check.stem: Which elements must bond to hydrogen for hydrogen bonding to occur?

options.text: Oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine
options.explanation: Only these highly electronegative atoms polarise the hydrogen enough for the link.

options.text: Carbon, sulfur or phosphorus
options.explanation: None of these pull electron density hard enough from hydrogen.

options.text: Sodium, potassium or calcium
options.explanation: These are metals, not the electronegative partners required.

options.text: Chlorine, bromine or iodine
options.explanation: Halogen bonds to hydrogen stay polar but fall short of hydrogen bonding strength.

check.stem: What does the hydrogen in a hydrogen bond reach toward?

options.text: A lone pair on an oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine of a neighbouring molecule
options.explanation: The exposed positive hydrogen links to a lone pair facing it.

options.text: The covalent bond of the neighbour
options.explanation: The link forms to a lone pair, not into a bond.

options.text: The neighbour's nucleus
options.explanation: Direct nuclear contact is not the mechanism.

options.text: Another hydrogen atom
options.explanation: Hydrogen-to-hydrogen contact is not hydrogen bonding.

check.stem: Why does a water molecule form two hydrogen bonds?

options.text: Its oxygen carries two lone pairs
options.explanation: Each lone pair can face one delta-positive hydrogen of a neighbour.

options.text: It has two hydrogen atoms only
options.explanation: Two hydrogens make it a donor, but the count of links formed is set by the lone pairs.

options.text: It is the smallest molecule available
options.explanation: Size does not set the bonding count.

options.text: Its hydrogen atoms are unusually negative
options.explanation: The hydrogens are delta-positive, not negative.

check.stem: Which ranking of hydrogen bonding is correct?

options.text: Strongest intermolecular attraction, yet weaker than any covalent bond
options.explanation: It tops the between-molecule ladder while staying about a tenth of a covalent bond.

options.text: Stronger than covalent bonds
options.explanation: Nothing between molecules beats the bonds inside them.

options.text: Weaker than induced dipole-dipole forces
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding sits at the top, not the bottom.

options.text: Equal in strength to permanent dipole-dipole forces
options.explanation: Hydrogen bonding is a strengthened sub-case, not an equal.

check.stem: Why does the hydrogen become strongly positive in an O-H bond?

options.text: Oxygen pulls the shared electrons toward itself
options.explanation: High electronegativity drains density from hydrogen, exposing its positive character.

options.text: Hydrogen donates its proton
options.explanation: The proton stays covalently held; only electron density shifts.

options.text: Oxygen repels the hydrogen nucleus
options.explanation: Repulsion is not the source of polarity.

options.text: The bond is ionic from the start
options.explanation: An O-H bond is polar covalent, not fully ionic.

check.stem: State the two requirements for hydrogen bonding between two molecules.
check.modelAnswer: One molecule must carry hydrogen covalently bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine, and the other molecule must present a lone pair on such an atom for the hydrogen to reach.

check.stem: Give the strength ladder from weakest to strongest for induced, permanent and hydrogen-bonded attractions.
check.modelAnswer: Induced dipole-dipole is weakest, permanent dipole-dipole sits in the middle, and hydrogen bonding is the strongest intermolecular attraction.

check.stem: Explain why hydrogen bonding counts as a special case of permanent dipole-dipole attraction.
check.modelAnswer: Both attractions run between fixed positive and negative ends of polar molecules; hydrogen bonding is the extreme version where electronegative atoms concentrate so much charge on hydrogen that a lone pair completes an unusually strong dipole link.

check.stem: Ethanoic acid pairs up through two hydrogen bonds per dimer. If one hydrogen bond is worth 25 kJ per mole, how much extra energy does forming the double bridge contribute per mole of dimer?
check.modelAnswer: Two hydrogen bonds at 25 kJ per mole each give 50 kJ per mole, which is why the dimer survives even in the gas phase.

glossary.definition: A force acting inside a single molecule, in practice a covalent bond of any order holding its atoms together.
A far weaker attraction acting between neighbouring molecules, deciding melting and boiling behaviour.
The weakest intermolecular attraction, made when a flickering electron cloud creates a temporary dipole that polarises a neighbour.
The strongest intermolecular attraction, formed where hydrogen bonded to oxygen, nitrogen or fluorine reaches a lone pair on a neighbouring molecule.
